items.title: MAXUS Pre-Reg Watch: Five Big Discounts Worth Knowing About
items.summary: MAXUS has become one of the more interesting value brands in the UK commercial vehicle market, with a range that now stretches from diesel and electric vans to pickups and large MPVs. Backed by SAIC Motor, it has steadily built its case around equipment, electrification and aggressive pricing. That value argument becomes…

The DELIVER 9 is no longer an unfamiliar Chinese newcomer. It has been on UK roads since 2020 and, after several years of fleet sales, has become a relatively common sight. This is a full-size large van with up to 12.9m³ of load space, a 2.0-litre diesel engine and a choice of front- or rear-wheel drive, putting it firmly into Transit, Boxer and Movano territory.

At £19,296 + VAT pre-reg, though, it costs considerably less than most equivalent large vans. For buyers who simply need a lot of usable van for their money, the DELIVER 9 makes a particularly strong value case.

Taken together, these five deals show how aggressively MAXUS is competing on value. The biggest reductions are on the eDELIVER 7 and DELIVER 9, but even the pickups and MIFA 7 are being advertised well below list price.

MAXUS may still lack the badge recognition of some established rivals, but at these pre-reg prices it becomes much harder to dismiss — particularly for buyers more interested in capability, equipment and usable range than the name on the grille.

Prices and specifications were correct at the time of publication and may change without notice. Pre-registered prices are based on advertised UK stock and may vary by dealer, specification and availability. RRP figures refer to official UK list prices; commercial vehicle prices are shown excluding VAT where stated. Images courtesy of MAXUS/SAIC Motor.

items.title: Peugeot 6008: The Flagship SUV Nobody Expected
items.summary: Stellantis’ Chinese story is increasingly dominated by Leapmotor, but another partnership is quietly becoming important again. Dongfeng has worked with Peugeot and Citroën in China for more than three decades, yet that relationship is often overlooked in today’s Stellantis narrative. Now that partnership has produced two particularly significant Peugeot concepts. Concept 6…
items.content_html:
Stellantis’ Chinese story is increasingly dominated by Leapmotor, but another partnership is quietly becoming important again. Dongfeng has worked with Peugeot and Citroën in China for more than three decades, yet that relationship is often overlooked in today’s Stellantis narrative.

Now that partnership has produced two particularly significant Peugeot concepts. Concept 6 previews a sleek, low-slung large car, while Concept 8 points towards a new flagship SUV developed through the Dongfeng-Peugeot partnership. Both are being developed towards production models expected to be built in China from 2027.

Concept 8 may soon become more relevant to Europe. Peugeot had previously indicated that neither Concept 6 nor Concept 8 was intended for the European market, making the latest development particularly curious. French Peugeot specialist Forum-Peugeot now reports that Concept 8 will be brought to France for October’s Paris Motor Show, citing a reliable source.

Concept 8 is intended to be a genuine halo model: a large electric flagship sitting above the 5008, with a production version expected to offer up to seven seats. Peugeot has not released its final dimensions, but its scale puts it much closer in concept to cars such as the Kia EV9 and Hyundai Ioniq 9 than to another conventional family SUV.

That leaves plenty of room above the existing 5008. At 4,791mm long, Peugeot’s current seven-seater is already slightly larger than a Chery Tiggo 8 and Skoda Kodiaq, yet starts at around £37,000 as a hybrid and £39,000 as an E-5008. A larger electric flagship beginning at roughly £60,000 could therefore sit comfortably above it while still undercutting the £65,000-plus EV9 and Ioniq 9.

Concepts 6 and 8 are already being developed towards production in China, with selected export markets also expected to receive the resulting models. Concept 8 is now reported to be heading for the Paris Motor Show, but there has been no equivalent announcement for Concept 6 — which is perhaps a pity.

The sleek fastback reads almost like a natural successor to the 508, Peugeot's previous halo model, which disappeared without a direct replacement as the brand increasingly centred its European range around the slightly smaller 408 crossover and its existing line of SUVs. Image: Peugeot

Peugeot also has good reason to test how far customers are prepared to follow it upmarket. Despite offering the 3008 and 5008 at considerably lower entry prices, British buyers have shown a strong appetite for higher specifications.

During the E-3008's first months on sale, 85% of UK customers chose the range-topping GT trim, compared with 60% across markets. Peugeot has since gone further, introducing an even richer GT Premium specification for both the 3008 and 5008.

Inside, our E-6008 interpretation moves Peugeot's i-Cockpit another step forward, building on the already high-quality cabin design of the current 3008 and 5008. Rather than reinventing it completely, we have imagined how that architecture could evolve for a more expensive flagship — including Peugeot's new Hypersquare steering control.

Hypersquare replaces the conventional steering wheel with a compact rectangular steer-by-wire controller, with no mechanical connection to the front wheels. It varies its response with speed and requires just 170 degrees of rotation in either direction at low speeds. Peugeot plans to introduce the technology on a production model from 2027.

It also feels particularly well suited to Peugeot. The existing i-Cockpit has already spent years positioning a small steering wheel beneath a high-mounted instrument display, so Hypersquare develops an established Peugeot idea rather than introducing an entirely unfamiliar driving position.

Visitors to the 2026 Paris Motor Show are expected to see Concept 8 alongside Peugeot's latest Hypersquare technology, with Peugeot also bringing the Polygon Concept that has acted as a rolling test bed for the technology. Polygon previews the next generation of Peugeot design and technology expected to feed into future models, including the next-generation 208.

That makes Hypersquare a particularly appropriate addition to our imagined E-6008: by the time a production Concept 8 derivative reaches showrooms, this radical-looking control could already be established Peugeot technology. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio — speculative Peugeot E-6008 interior rendering.

From the rear, Concept 8's potential as a Peugeot flagship becomes particularly clear. It is a striking design, but not one that feels completely detached from the brand's current direction. More importantly, there appears to be a plausible European market for it. Peugeot's own customers have already shown a willingness to move towards the more expensive end of its existing range.

That makes next month's Paris Motor Show particularly interesting. Peugeot will put considerable emphasis on its future design and technology, including Hypersquare and the Polygon Concept, as Stellantis uses the show to present a much broader vision of where its brands are heading.

For TNY, two questions stand out. Will Hypersquare become a defining feature that spreads across several Peugeot models, rather than simply appearing on one new generation of car? And, perhaps more importantly, why is Concept 8 reportedly being brought to Paris?

If it were simply a China-focused design exercise, its appearance at Peugeot's home motor show would be less significant. Instead, Paris gives Peugeot an opportunity to put the car directly in front of European customers and gauge the reaction to something considerably larger and more expensive than today's 5008.

We don't yet know whether that will ultimately result in an E-6008 — or whether Europe will receive Concept 8's production descendant at all. But the ingredients are increasingly plausible. If Peugeot wants a flagship again, Concept 8 could provide it with a very different successor to the role once occupied by the 508. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio — speculative Peugeot E-6008 rendering.

items.title: Nissan Pixo: Could Britain's Former Cheapest Car Make an Electric Comeback?
items.summary: When the Nissan Pixo arrived in the UK in 2009, it quickly established itself at the very bottom of Britain's new-car market. For the majority of its short life, it was Britain's cheapest new car — a position that became an important part of the little Nissan's identity. Then, in 2013, Dacia…
items.content_html:
When the Nissan Pixo arrived in the UK in 2009, it quickly established itself at the very bottom of Britain's new-car market. For the majority of its short life, it was Britain's cheapest new car — a position that became an important part of the little Nissan's identity.

Then, in 2013, Dacia changed the game. The considerably larger Sandero arrived with its now-famous £5,995 starting price, bringing the Pixo's time at the bottom of the market to an abrupt end and resetting expectations of just how much car Britain's cheapest models could offer.

Today, Dacia is once again responsible for Britain's cheapest new car with the Spring. This time, however, a reborn Pixo wouldn't necessarily be fighting Dacia's approach to cheap motoring from the outside. By using the small-EV programme underpinning the new Renault Twingo E-Tech and upcoming Dacia Spring, Nissan could create a genuinely low-cost electric car of its own, sitting substantially below the current Micra EV.

It would return the Pixo to exactly the part of the market where people remember it: simple, small and among the cheapest new cars in Britain. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio

The original Pixo was already a product of collaboration. Rather than developing an ultra-low-cost city car from scratch, Nissan turned to Suzuki, with the Pixo closely related to the contemporary Alto and both cars produced by Maruti Suzuki in India.

That makes the idea of a Renault-developed successor rather more appropriate than it might initially appear. The badge, partner and technology would change, but the philosophy would be remarkably similar: take an existing small-car programme, give it a Nissan identity and use the economies of scale to put Nissan back at the cheapest end of the market.

Nearly two decades later, globalisation has only made that approach more common. Nissan already shares technology extensively with Renault, while the next Twingo and upcoming Dacia Spring provide something its own European range currently lacks — the foundations for a genuinely inexpensive A-segment EV. Image: Nissan

There is something remarkably familiar about three manufacturers sharing the cost of creating a new generation of affordable city cars.

Twenty years ago, Toyota joined forces with Peugeot and Citroën to create the Aygo, 107 and C1. One Japanese manufacturer and two European brands shared the basic engineering and production of three closely related cars, helping make them cheap to buy, cheap to run and viable to produce.

Two decades later, the same Japanese-European formula could be coming back in electric form. This time it is Nissan representing Japan, alongside European partners Renault and Dacia. The new Twingo and upcoming Spring already share their small-EV foundations, while Nissan's upcoming entry-level EV is clearly heading in the same direction, with Twingo-like proportions and a remarkably similar window line.

If that Nissan becomes the Pixo, the parallels will be difficult to miss. Once again, two European brands and one Japanese manufacturer would be sharing the expensive foundations of three distinct city cars, spreading development costs while giving each its own design and identity.


For a while, Europe's city-car segment looked close to extinction. Tiny petrol cars offered manufacturers slim profit margins, while increasingly expensive emissions and safety requirements made developing a new generation difficult to justify. Now electrification and shared platforms are giving the class another chance.

Toyota's Aygo X has gone hybrid, the Fiat 500e has been joined by a new 500 Hybrid, while the Leapmotor T03, Hyundai Inster and Dacia Spring have already pushed small EVs towards genuinely affordable territory.

Next come the new Renault Twingo E-Tech and upcoming Spring, followed by small Hyundai and Kia EVs and Volkswagen Group's new entry-level Volkswagen and Škoda models. Suddenly, Britain could have a surprisingly crowded selection of city cars competing around or below £20,000.

A new Pixo could give Nissan something its emerging electric range currently lacks: a genuinely low-cost entry point. Sitting comfortably below £20,000, it could focus on compact dimensions, simplicity and everyday urban use, leaving the new Micra EV as the more substantial and desirable supermini.

The Leaf then gives Nissan another fresh electric option for buyers wanting something different again, with greater range and a more crossover-like approach. Together, Pixo, Micra and Leaf could give Nissan three distinct new EVs covering different prices and priorities at the smaller end of the market.

A new Pixo wouldn't need to reinvent Nissan's smallest car. In many ways, the strongest argument for bringing the name back is that it could follow exactly the same philosophy as the original: borrow the expensive foundations from elsewhere, add enough Nissan identity to make the result distinctive, and concentrate on keeping the price low.

With the Micra and Leaf already giving Nissan two fresh electric models further up the range, a Pixo priced comfortably below them could complete one of the most convincing small-EV line-ups on the UK market.

The technology would be completely different from 2009, but the objective would be remarkably familiar. If Nissan really wants to put an electric car back near the bottom of Britain's price lists, the Pixo might be exactly the right name for it. Image: The New Yardstick Design Studio.

items.title: Two Cylinders Were Once Enough: The Rise and Fall of the Two-Cylinder Car
items.summary: For much of the car's history, two cylinders were enough. Small, light and relatively simple, twin-cylinder engines powered everything from basic family transport to some of the world's most distinctive small cars. The Citroën 2CV, Fiat 500 and Subaru 360 helped mobilise millions, while later examples showed just how far the idea…
items.content_html:
Morgan Three Wheeler

Citroën 2CV

Few cars are more closely associated with two cylinders than the Citroën 2CV. Launched in 1948, it was designed as simple, inexpensive transport for rural France, combining an air-cooled flat-twin engine with exceptionally soft suspension and a lightweight body. Early cars produced just 9 hp from 375cc, but the engine gradually grew in capacity and power, eventually reaching 602cc in later versions.


Fiat 500

Launched in 1957, the Fiat Nuova 500 approached affordable motoring from a very different direction to the 2CV. At barely three metres long, it was designed to squeeze families and everyday transport into the crowded streets of post-war Italy.

Behind the rear seats sat a tiny air-cooled two-cylinder engine. The original 479cc unit produced just 13 hp, but low weight and extraordinary simplicity made outright power far less important. Later versions gained larger and more powerful engines while retaining the basic twin-cylinder layout.


Subaru 360

Launched in 1958, the Subaru 360 brought the two-cylinder formula to Japan's rapidly developing car market. Built to comply with Japan's kei-car regulations, it measured less than three metres long yet was designed to accommodate four adults — an impressive piece of packaging for the period.

Its rear-mounted 356cc two-cylinder, two-stroke engine kept the mechanical package compact, while lightweight monocoque construction drew on Subaru's aircraft-engineering heritage. Its rounded shape also earned it the affectionate Japanese nickname “Ladybug.”


Fiat 126

Launched in 1972 as the successor to the 500, the Fiat 126 carried the company's two-cylinder formula into a new generation. Its squarer body looked considerably more modern, but underneath remained the familiar rear-engined, air-cooled twin-cylinder layout that had helped make its predecessor so accessible.

Early cars used a 594cc engine, later growing to 652cc, while Polish production transformed the 126 into an important people's car in its own right. More than 3.3 million were eventually produced in Poland, where it became affectionately known as the Maluch, or “little one.”

Remarkably, production continued until 2000. The 126 therefore kept the traditional two-cylinder people's car alive a full decade after the Citroën 2CV had disappeared. Image: Tony Harrison / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)


Citroën Visa

By the time the Citroën Visa arrived in 1978, the company's air-cooled flat-twin had already powered generations of affordable cars. Alongside the 2CV, variants of the engine had appeared in the Ami and Dyane, making two cylinders a familiar part of Citroën's identity.

The Visa was a much more modern proposition, sharing its basic platform with the Peugeot 104. Entry-level Spécial and Club versions nevertheless retained a 652cc evolution of Citroën's flat-twin, while more powerful Visas adopted four-cylinder engines.

It proved to be one of the twin's final appearances in a new Citroën design. The two-cylinder Visa disappeared during the 1980s, remarkably leaving the much older 2CV to carry the flat-twin into 1990 — more than four decades after its introduction. Image: Citroën / Stellantis


Tata Nano

When the Tata Nano reached production in 2009, two cylinders returned for a purpose that would have been familiar decades earlier: making car ownership more accessible. Developed for India, the Nano was conceived as an affordable alternative for families relying on motorcycles and scooters.

Its rear-mounted 624cc petrol engine produced around 35 bhp, driving through a four-speed manual gearbox. Combined with a lightweight body and tiny dimensions, the simple two-cylinder layout helped Tata keep manufacturing costs, weight and fuel consumption down.

The Nano never achieved the huge sales originally envisaged, and production ended in 2018. Nevertheless, it remains a fascinating modern echo of earlier people's cars: a genuinely new vehicle using two cylinders primarily because simplicity and affordability still mattered. Image: Tata Nano — High Contrast / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0 DE)


Fiat 500 TwinAir

In 2010, Fiat returned the two-cylinder engine to mainstream European motoring with the 500 TwinAir. Rather than chasing absolute simplicity, this time the idea was downsizing: using turbocharging and modern engine management to extract useful performance from a tiny engine.

The 875cc turbocharged TwinAir initially produced 85 hp, but Fiat later pushed the tiny engine to 105 hp in the 500. That was remarkable output from just two cylinders, while its distinctive offbeat soundtrack became part of the appeal. Fiat promoted strong official economy and CO₂ figures as major advantages of the compact design.

TwinAir later appeared in several Fiat Group models, but the 500 was its natural home. It demonstrated how sophisticated the two-cylinder engine had become, although real-world economy could fall short of the remarkable official figures. Image: FIAT / Stellantis


Alfa Romeo MiTo TwinAir

If the Fiat 500 was a natural home for the TwinAir engine, the Alfa Romeo MiTo pushed the two-cylinder idea into relatively upmarket territory. Introduced to the UK in 2012, it combined Alfa styling and premium-supermini ambitions with Fiat Group's tiny 875cc turbocharged twin.

What made the MiTo interesting was the contrast. Two-cylinder engines had traditionally belonged to basic cars built around low cost, yet here one appeared in an Alfa Romeo competing with increasingly sophisticated European superminis. Buyers could specify leather, upgraded technology and distinctive styling around one of the smallest engines available.


BMW i3 REx

The BMW i3 took the two-cylinder engine somewhere entirely new. Launched in 2013, the innovative electric hatchback could be ordered as a Range Extender, adding a compact 647cc two-cylinder petrol engine derived from BMW's C 650 GT maxi-scooter.

Unlike a conventional hybrid, the engine never drove the wheels. Instead, it acted as a generator, producing electricity when the battery became depleted. This allowed BMW to extend the i3's usable range while retaining electric propulsion, easing range anxiety when public charging infrastructure was still developing.


Suzuki Celerio

In 2015, Suzuki found another reason for using just two cylinders: extreme diesel efficiency. Developed specifically for India, the Celerio DDiS 125 used Suzuki's first internally developed diesel engine, a tiny 793cc two-cylinder turbo producing 47 hp and 125 Nm.

Performance was modest, but economy was extraordinary. Maruti Suzuki quoted 27.62 km/l, equivalent to roughly 78 mpg (UK), making it India's most fuel-efficient production car at launch. The all-aluminium engine and lightweight Celerio showed how far downsized diesel engineering could be pushed.

The experiment proved short-lived as small diesels increasingly fell from favour. Nevertheless, the Celerio remains one of the strangest final chapters in two-cylinder history: a conventional five-door hatchback powered by an exceptionally small turbodiesel. Image: Maruti Suzuki India / Suzuki


Morgan 3 Wheeler

More than a century after H.F.S. Morgan built his first three-wheeler, the company returned to the same basic idea in 2011. The modern Morgan 3 Wheeler placed a large S&S V-twin prominently ahead of the front axle, immediately recalling the machines that had established Morgan's reputation.

This time, however, two cylinders had little to do with making transport affordable. The exposed engine was deliberately theatrical, contributing vibration, noise and mechanical character to a car designed primarily to make ordinary journeys feel special. Its unusual layout became central to the experience.

Production ended in 2021, and its successor, the Super 3, adopted a Ford three-cylinder engine. It was a fitting final flourish for the two-cylinder car: returning to its earliest roots purely for enjoyment. Image: Morgan Motor Company

Conclusion

Two-cylinder cars probably aren't coming back. Modern emissions requirements, refinement expectations and electrification leave increasingly little reason to accept their inherent compromises.

Yet their influence is enormous. From inexpensive transport for post-war families to turbocharged Fiats, an electrified BMW and a deliberately eccentric Morgan, two cylinders repeatedly proved capable of far more than their size suggested. Their disappearance closes one of motoring's most distinctive engineering chapters.

items.title: Car Depreciation: Why Predicted Resale Values Don't Tell the Whole Story
items.summary: Six months ago, nobody knew quite what the British summer would bring. Forecasts and long-range predictions could point us in a direction, but they couldn't tell us what would actually happen. Fast-forward to August and England and Wales have experienced their driest July on record, with drought affecting much of the country.
items.content_html:
Suzuki Ignis (2023)

RRP From: £17,349
Pre-Reg From: c.£16,500
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.51% / c.£8,850
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£12,000 / c.69%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.73%

The Ignis demonstrates how affordable, distinctive cars can outperform conventional depreciation forecasts. A predicted three-year value of around £8,850 suggested buyers could expect to lose almost half of the original £17,349 list price. In reality, comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for around £12,000, retaining roughly 69% of their original value. Even against a more realistic pre-registered purchase price of around £16,500, that represents 73% retained. Limited supply, low running costs and the Ignis's unusual position as a tiny, lightweight crossover appear to have helped values remain remarkably resilient.


Fiat Panda (2023)

RRP From: £14,740
Pre-Reg From: c.£13,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.48% / c.£7,100
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£9,000 / c.61%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.69%

The Panda tells a remarkably similar story to the Ignis. Its predicted three-year value of around £7,100 suggested a fairly typical depreciation curve, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for around £9,000, retaining roughly 61% of their original list price and 69% of a typical pre-registered price. Much of that resilience comes from the Panda occupying an increasingly scarce position in the market: a genuinely small, affordable mild-hybrid city car with relatively few direct alternatives. With new city cars disappearing and demand remaining healthy, used buyers have fewer places to turn.


Toyota Yaris (2023)

RRP From: £22,125
Pre-Reg From: c.£20,500
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.57% / c.£12,600
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£14,000 / c.63%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.68%

The Yaris was always expected to perform relatively well, but even its strong predicted residual value appears to have underestimated demand. Comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for around £14,000, retaining roughly 63% of their original list price and 68% of a typical pre-registered price. Toyota's reputation for reliability and the Yaris's efficient hybrid powertrain, low running costs and popularity with owners all help explain its resilience. Buyers should be careful when comparing cheaper advertisements, however, as the UK used market contains numerous imported Japanese-market Yaris models that can distort headline asking prices.


Vauxhall Corsa (2023)

RRP From: £18,585
Pre-Reg From: c.£15,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.41% / c.£7,600
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£9,000 / c.48%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.60%

The Corsa also performed better than predicted, with comparable 2023 cars retaining around 48% of their original list price rather than the forecast 41%. However, the more interesting figure is what happens when substantial new-car discounts are taken into account. Pre-registered examples could be bought for around £15,000 rather than the £18,585 list price, meaning a car now retailing for approximately £9,000 has retained around 60% of that more realistic purchase price. It demonstrates why depreciation measured purely against RRP can exaggerate the amount of money an individual buyer actually loses.


Volkswagen ID.3 (2023)

RRP From: £37,115
Pre-Reg From: c.£32,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.52% / c.£19,300
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£14,500 / c.39%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.45%

The ID.3 shows the opposite side of the story. Its predicted three-year value of around £19,300 suggested it would retain 52% of its original list price, yet comparable 2023 cars are now retailing for closer to £14,500, or just 39%. Even allowing for pre-registered discounts, that represents only around 45% retained. Electric cars have proved particularly difficult to forecast as prices, technology and demand have changed rapidly, while German models have not always delivered the residual-value strength traditionally expected of them. The ID.3 demonstrates how an apparently reassuring forecast can quickly become outdated.


Mazda 3 (2023)

RRP From: £23,945
Pre-Reg From: c.£22,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.48% / c.£11,500
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£14,500 / c.61%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.66%

The Mazda 3 is another car that appears to have been underestimated. Its relatively modest £23,945 starting price gave it a useful head start, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for around £14,500, retaining roughly 61% of their original value rather than the predicted 48%. Even against a typical pre-registered price of around £22,000, approximately 66% remains. A comfortable, well-built interior, strong standard equipment and an increasingly unusual position as a conventional family hatchback have helped make the Mazda 3 considerably more resilient than the original forecasts suggested.


SEAT Arona (2023)

RRP From: £21,695
Pre-Reg From: c.£18,500
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.45% / c.£9,760
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£11,000 / c.51%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.59%

The Arona has also performed better than its original forecast suggested. A predicted three-year value of around £9,760 represented just 45% of its original list price, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for approximately £11,000, or 51%. More importantly, pre-registered examples could be bought for around £18,500, increasing the proportion retained to roughly 59%. Sharing much of its underlying technology with Volkswagen Group models gives the Arona proven German engineering without the typically higher German-brand RRP, while its practical interior and compact dimensions have helped maintain healthy used demand.


Nissan Juke (2023)

RRP From: £20,985
Pre-Reg From: c.£17,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.45% / c.£9,440
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£11,000 / c.52%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.65%

The Juke is another example where substantial pre-registered discounts worked against the original depreciation forecast. Its predicted three-year value of around £9,440 represented just 45% of the £20,985 list price, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for approximately £11,000. More importantly, pre-registered examples could be bought for around £17,000, meaning roughly 65% of that more realistic purchase price remains today. Strong demand for small SUVs has undoubtedly helped, but the Juke demonstrates how buying at a substantial discount when new can completely change the depreciation calculation.


Dacia Jogger (2023)

RRP From: £17,165
Pre-Reg From: c.£16,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.55% / c.£9,440
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£12,500 / c.73%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.78%

The Jogger is one of the clearest examples of the original predictions underestimating the market. Despite already starting at an unusually low £17,165, it was predicted to retain around £9,440 after three years. Comparable 2023 cars are instead retailing for approximately £12,500 — an impressive 73% of the original RRP and 78% of a typical pre-registered purchase price. Its combination of seven seats, enormous practicality and genuinely affordable pricing remains difficult to replicate, leaving used buyers with relatively few alternatives. Dacia didn't simply make the Jogger cheap; it gave it a niche that has proved remarkably resistant to depreciation.


MG HS (2023)

RRP From: £23,495
Pre-Reg From: c.£18,500
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.46% / c.£10,810
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£12,000 / c.51%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.65%

The HS is another case where the original RRP tells only part of the story. Its predicted three-year value of around £10,810 represented 46% of list price, while comparable 2023 cars are actually retailing for around £12,000. More importantly, pre-registered examples could be bought for approximately £18,500. That means a buyer paying the discounted price has lost around £6,500 over three years — equivalent to just £181 per month in depreciation. For a spacious, well-equipped family SUV, that makes the HS's real-world ownership cost considerably more impressive than its predicted residual value suggested.


Hyundai Santa Fe (2023)

RRP From: £42,890
Pre-Reg From: c.£38,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.54% / c.£23,160
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£27,000 / c.63%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.71%

The Santa Fe is a particularly strong result for Hyundai. Its predicted three-year value of around £23,160 represented 54% of the original list price, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for approximately £27,000, retaining a much healthier 63%. Against a typical pre-registered price of around £38,000, that rises to an impressive 71%. The Santa Fe's combination of genuine seven-seat practicality, generous equipment, strong hybrid options and increasingly premium feel has clearly translated into used-market desirability, demonstrating how far Hyundai has progressed from its old reputation as primarily a value-focused brand.


Range Rover Velar (2023)

RRP From: £55,330
Pre-Reg From: c.£51,500
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.62% / c.£34,300
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£28,000 / c.51%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.54%

The Velar shows that a premium badge doesn't automatically guarantee strong residual values. It was predicted to retain around 62% of its original £55,330 list price after three years, yet comparable 2023 cars are now retailing for closer to £28,000, or 51%. Even against a typical pre-registered price, only around 54% remains. This isn't necessarily a wider Land Rover problem — the larger Range Rover Sport has generally proved more resilient. Instead, the Velar demonstrates how individual models can perform very differently, and why paying for a premium badge doesn't always guarantee a better return when it comes to resale.


Alfa Romeo Giulia (2023)

RRP From: £43,259
Pre-Reg From: c.£36,500
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.41% / c.£17,700
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£28,000 / c.65%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.77%

The Giulia is one of the biggest surprises in our comparison. A predicted three-year value of around £17,700 suggested it would retain just 41% of its original list price, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for around £28,000 — roughly 65%. Against a typical pre-registered purchase price of £36,500, an impressive 77% remains. It also challenges the assumption that an SUV is automatically the safer place to put your money. Despite being a traditional sports saloon in an increasingly SUV-dominated market, the Giulia has comfortably outperformed the experts' expectations.


Citroën C5 X (2023)

RRP From: £28,670
Pre-Reg From: c.£23,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.44% / c.£12,615
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£13,500 / c.47%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.59%

The C5 X is a particularly interesting example because its headline depreciation has landed fairly close to the original forecast. A three-year value of around £12,615 was predicted, while comparable 2023 cars are now retailing for roughly £13,500. But that misses the effect of the substantial discounts available when new. Pre-registered cars could be bought for around £23,000 rather than the £28,670 RRP, meaning approximately 59% of that more realistic purchase price remains today. For such a large, comfortable and distinctive family car, buying at the right price has made the C5 X a surprisingly strong value proposition over three years.


Lexus ES (2023)

RRP From: £40,000
Pre-Reg From: c.£36,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.44% / c.£17,600
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£27,500 / c.69%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.76%

The ES provides further evidence of just how valuable Toyota Group's reputation for hybrid efficiency and reliability can be in the used market. A predicted three-year value of around £17,600 suggested it would retain only 44% of its original £40,000 list price, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for approximately £27,500 — an impressive 69%. Against a typical pre-registered price of around £36,000, that rises to 76%. Its proven hybrid technology, excellent refinement and strong reputation for dependability have helped the ES comfortably outperform the original predictions.


Volvo V90 (2023)

RRP From: £50,315
Pre-Reg From: c.£45,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.49% / c.£24,655
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£30,000 / c.60%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.67%

The V90 is another traditional body style that has performed considerably better than expected. Its predicted three-year value of around £24,655 represented 49% of the original £50,315 list price, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for approximately £30,000, or 60%. Against a typical pre-registered price of around £45,000, roughly 67% remains. Large estates may have fallen out of fashion as SUVs have taken over the market, but the V90's combination of space, comfort, distinctive Scandinavian design and increasingly limited competition appears to have helped support demand for good used examples.


Mercedes-Benz EQS (2023)

RRP From: £102,160
Pre-Reg From: c.£102,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.53% / c.£54,140
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£43,000 / c.42%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.42%

The EQS is where the numbers become difficult to ignore. Industry experts predicted a three-year value of around £54,140, yet comparable 2023 cars are now retailing for closer to £43,000 — just 42% of the original £102,160 list price. Unlike several cars in our comparison, there was also little pre-registered discount to cushion that fall, meaning an early buyer could realistically have lost around £59,000 in three years — roughly £1,640 every month in depreciation alone. Rapidly developing EV technology, a six-figure starting price and a difficult used market for luxury electric cars have made the EQS one of our most dramatic examples.


Porsche Taycan 4S (2023)

RRP From: £90,755
Pre-Reg From: c.£90,000
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.75% / c.£68,070
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£42,000 / c.46%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.47%

The Taycan 4S is perhaps the most striking example in our entire comparison. Industry forecasts suggested it could retain around 75% of its £90,755 list price after three years, putting its predicted value at approximately £68,070. In reality, comparable cars are now retailing for around £42,000 — just 46% of the original RRP. It highlights several recurring weaknesses in depreciation forecasting at once: premium German cars, large luxury saloons and rapidly evolving EVs can all be overestimated. The Taycan remains hugely desirable, but desirability and an expensive badge haven't translated into the residual values experts expected.


BMW M3 (2023)

RRP From: £81,195
Pre-Reg From: c.£69,995
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.50% / c.£40,600
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£56,000 / c.69%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.80%

The M3 proves that German performance cars don't automatically follow the same depreciation story. Industry forecasts suggested a three-year value of around £40,600, yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for approximately £56,000 — an impressive 69% of RRP and 80% of a typical pre-registered price. Part of that resilience may come from an increasingly unusual position in the market. As traditional rivals have become heavier, electrified or plug-in hybrid performance cars, the six-cylinder M3 has retained a more focused character, helping push it into a distinctive segment of its own.


Toyota GR Yaris (2023)

RRP From: £32,205
Pre-Reg From: c.£32,205
3yr / 36k Predicted Value: c.60% / c.£19,300
3yr / 36k Actual Retail Value: c.£29,000 / c.90%
Value Retained vs Pre-Reg Price: c.90%

The GR Yaris is the standout winner in our comparison, and another major result for Toyota Group. Industry forecasts suggested it would retain around 60% of its £32,205 list price after three years — already a strong prediction — yet comparable 2023 cars are still retailing for approximately £29,000, representing an extraordinary 90%. With virtually no meaningful pre-registered discount to change the calculation, that resilience is genuine. Limited supply, enormous enthusiast demand and its rally-inspired engineering have made the GR Yaris far more than another hot hatch, with used values comfortably outperforming even the experts' optimistic expectations.

What Does This Tell Us About Depreciation?

The biggest lesson is that depreciation forecasts are useful guides, not guarantees. Across our 20 cars, some predictions proved remarkably pessimistic, while others underestimated losses by tens of thousands of pounds.

More importantly, RRP doesn't always represent what buyers actually paid. Pre-registered discounts can completely transform the ownership calculation, while scarcity, reliability, changing technology and simple used-car demand can push values in directions the experts never anticipated. The GR Yaris retaining around 90% while the Taycan 4S retains 46% demonstrates just how unpredictable the market can be.

The answer isn't to ignore depreciation forecasts — it's to never rely on them alone.

Prices and used-car values shown in this article are approximate UK retail figures and were correct at the time of research. Used-car prices can change quickly depending on mileage, specification, condition, location and wider market demand. Pre-registered prices are representative advertised figures and may not have been available across every specification or throughout the entire period shown. Predicted three-year values are industry estimates based on approximately 36,000 miles and should not be treated as guaranteed future values. Actual retail values are based on representative UK-market vehicles of a comparable age and mileage, excluding imports, insurance-category vehicles and obvious market outliers.
Unless otherwise stated, vehicle images are manufacturer press photographs and remain the copyright of their respective owners. Images are used for editorial and informational purposes.

items.title: Hyundai's 100-Car Plan: What Comes Next for One of the World's Fastest-Changing Car Makers?
items.summary: Twenty years ago, Hyundai was still fighting to prove that it could match the established European and Japanese brands. Today, that description feels almost unrecognisable. Hyundai has become a genuinely global manufacturer, producing everything from affordable small cars to sophisticated EVs, large SUVs and increasingly serious performance models. Now it wants to…
items.content_html:
Twenty years ago, Hyundai was still fighting to prove that it could match the established European and Japanese brands. Today, that description feels almost unrecognisable. Hyundai has become a genuinely global manufacturer, producing everything from affordable small cars to sophisticated EVs, large SUVs and increasingly serious performance models.

Now it wants to grow again.

Hyundai has announced plans to launch or substantially refresh more than 100 vehicles globally by 2030, including 58 launches in North America, 49 in Korea and 41 in Europe. More importantly, many won't simply replace existing cars: Hyundai says it intends to enter new segments and target the ‘white spaces’ where its range is currently underrepresented.

The numbers are huge, but they do not mean Hyundai is about to offer the same enormous range everywhere. Increasingly, Hyundai is developing its line-up around individual markets: North America wants larger SUVs, hybrids and EREVs; India remains heavily focused on affordable, locally produced models; China demands increasingly competitive electrified products; while Europe needs smaller cars, efficient hybrids and EVs that work within tighter streets, emissions rules and household budgets. Hyundai itself says Europe will gain five all-new SUV and light-commercial vehicles as it pushes EV sales towards 420,000 annually by 2030.

The Inster is an easy car to like. Its funky styling gives it genuine character, while clever touches such as sliding rear seats help it extract surprising versatility from its tiny footprint. With up to 229 miles of WLTP range, Hyundai has also shown that a small EV needn't be restricted to short urban journeys.

But there is a problem: the Inster isn't particularly cheap for something so small. It evolved from the Korean-market petrol Casper rather than starting life as a clean-sheet European EV, and that becomes increasingly relevant as the competition develops. The larger Citroën ë-C3 and Fiat Grande Panda offer considerably more conventional family-car space, with both being offered with starting prices below that of the Inster.

Commercial vehicles are one of the most obvious ‘white spaces’ Hyundai could target in Europe, but it wouldn't actually be new territory for the brand. The old iLoad gave Hyundai a genuine medium-sized panel van in the UK, while the closely related i800 turned the same basic formula into an eight-seat passenger model. Both arrived when Hyundai had considerably less pulling power in Europe than it does today.

Our Staria-based proposal revisits that idea for a very different Hyundai. A panel van could put the badge back into the commercial market, while a passenger version could provide a genuinely spacious alternative to the SUVs that now dominate Hyundai's range.

There is also a much stronger industrial foundation behind the idea today. Kia's new PV5 already demonstrates what Hyundai Motor Group can do with a modern purpose-developed electric commercial vehicle, offered in both Cargo and Passenger forms.

The new Tucson is perhaps the clearest indication of how quickly Hyundai is moving. The international model has grown substantially, stretching to around 4,700mm long, with a longer wheelbase and a noticeably more substantial, upmarket presence.

Europe is likely to require a slightly different approach. Hyundai already produces different Tucson dimensions for different global markets, and a European version measuring around 4,600mm would make sense — still representing a meaningful increase over today's car without becoming unnecessarily large for European roads. For now, however, that figure should be treated as our expectation rather than a confirmed specification.

What's particularly striking is that the outgoing Tucson hardly feels old. The current generation only arrived in 2020 and received a substantial facelift for 2024, including an extensively redesigned interior.

Growing the Tucson creates another white space in Hyundai's European range. The Kona is 4,350mm long, while our expected European Tucson could approach 4,600mm. As the Tucson grows and moves further upmarket, the distance between Hyundai's two core SUVs becomes increasingly noticeable.

Kia demonstrates just how much room there is to work with here. In an even tighter section of the market, it has the XCeed, Niro and Sportage, each approaching the family crossover brief differently rather than simply duplicating one another.

That's where our Hyundai Sonoma comes in. Named after Sonoma, California, it follows the geographic naming convention already established by Kona, Tucson and Santa Fe. But rather than simply adding another SUV to the range, our Sonoma is designed to fill the space Hyundai's existing models are beginning to leave behind.

The Kona would remain the stylish, efficiency-led compact choice, while the incoming Tucson becomes larger, more sophisticated and increasingly upmarket. Sonoma would take the middle ground: a straightforward family SUV around the size of a Renault Austral, with hybrid power, a practical interior, a useful boot and an emphasis on affordability.

Hyundai's expansion doesn't have to be limited to filling practical gaps. The N performance brand has developed from a handful of hot versions of ordinary Hyundais into an increasingly important part of the company's identity, and Hyundai now wants global N sales to reach around 100,000 cars annually.

Reaching that scale creates room for N to become much broader. Cars such as the Ioniq 5 N and Ioniq 6 N can provide the volume, while more specialised models could build an identity that isn't entirely dependent on turning existing Hyundai models into faster ones.

Our N74 explores what that could look like. It draws inspiration from the 1974 Hyundai Pony Coupé Concept, the Giorgetto Giugiaro-designed wedge that has become an increasingly important part of Hyundai's design history. Hyundai has already revisited those ideas with the spectacular N Vision 74 concept; our proposal takes the next step, imagining those influences distilled into a production N sports car.

It wouldn't need enormous sales to justify its existence. Its job would be to give N a recognisable halo of its own, while making everything beneath it more desirable.

It is easy, particularly from a European perspective, to think of Hyundai simply as the Korean company behind cars such as the i10, Tucson and Ioniq 5. But that dramatically understates the scale of the organisation behind the badge.

Hyundai sits within a vast industrial and mobility ecosystem. Hyundai Motor Group encompasses Hyundai, Kia and Genesis, but its reach extends far beyond passenger cars. Hyundai Rotem builds trains, metros and high-speed rail technology; Hyundai Mobis develops components, electrification and vehicle technology; Hyundai produces buses and heavy commercial vehicles; and the group has invested heavily in hydrogen, software and future mobility. It also owns a controlling stake in robotics specialist Boston Dynamics.

That wider picture matters when considering Hyundai's 100-car plan. This isn't a relatively small manufacturer suddenly attempting an enormous expansion. Hyundai has access to manufacturing scale, battery and electrification expertise, commercial vehicles, robotics, software, hydrogen technology and an enormous global supply chain.

The transformation of its passenger cars over the past 20 years is impressive, but it represents only one part of what Hyundai has become. Increasingly, this is a global mobility and technology group with the resources to compete across almost every part of transportation.

That growing strength creates an awkward question for Genesis. Hyundai and Kia have both moved dramatically upmarket, with increasingly sophisticated interiors, distinctive designs and some of the group's most advanced electric technology. Simply offering something slightly more luxurious with a Genesis badge is becoming harder to justify.

The GV60 demonstrates the problem particularly clearly. It shares its E-GMP foundations with the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6, yet occupies a more expensive premium position. Meanwhile, Hyundai's new Ioniq 3 brings some surprisingly Genesis-like design themes to a much smaller and more affordable EV. The boundaries within the group are becoming increasingly blurred.

The pictured GV60 Magma should provide some separation. Yet even here, the numbers illustrate the challenge. It produces 641bhp and reaches 0–62mph in 3.4 seconds — exactly the same headline power and acceleration figures quoted for the Hyundai Ioniq 6 N.

That doesn't make the Magma a bad proposition; Genesis can differentiate it through materials, refinement, exclusivity and the ownership experience. But when Hyundai itself can produce something equally spectacular on paper, Genesis needs to offer more than additional luxury and a different badge.

The incoming GV90 points towards a much clearer future for Genesis. Rather than sitting slightly above an equivalent Hyundai or Kia, this is a genuine flagship: an enormous electric luxury SUV designed to give Genesis a presence at the very top of the market.

That immediately creates meaningful separation. The Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Kia EV9 are already large three-row electric SUVs, but they remain fundamentally spacious family cars. The GV90 goes considerably further, placing greater emphasis on rear-seat luxury, materials, technology and the sense of occasion expected from a flagship.

The range-topping GV90 Neolun demonstrates just how far Genesis is prepared to take that idea. Its pillarless coach-door arrangement has made the transition from concept to production, creating a huge opening into the cabin without a conventional fixed B-pillar. The standard GV90 retains conventional doors, leaving this deliberately extravagant feature for the flagship version.

This is where Genesis makes considerably more sense. It doesn't need to build a slightly more luxurious alternative to every Hyundai. Instead, it can use the group's enormous engineering resources to create cars that Hyundai and Kia simply don't offer.

An Ioniq 9 can be an excellent large family EV without threatening the GV90, because the two have fundamentally different jobs.

The G90 provides another example of where Genesis can operate without treading on Hyundai's toes. At more than 5.2 metres long in standard form, this is a genuinely enormous luxury saloon, with the space, technology and opulence to target traditional flagships such as the BMW 7 Series and Mercedes-Benz S-Class.

It isn't currently offered in the UK, where the G80 instead gives Genesis a large executive saloon alongside its SUV-heavy range, but the G90 demonstrates the potential above it.

This isn't an Ioniq 6 with nicer materials. The G90 is designed as much around being driven in as driving yourself, with huge rear-seat accommodation and a sense of occasion that Hyundai doesn't attempt to replicate.

That leaves the Ioniq 6 free to be a distinctive, relatively attainable electric saloon, while Genesis can go larger, more luxurious and considerably more opulent.

Alongside the GV90, it suggests the answer to the Genesis problem: don't sit just above Hyundai — give Genesis room to sit properly beyond it. Image credit: Genesis Motor


What Comes Next for Hyundai?

Hyundai's 100-car plan is ultimately about much more than launching an extraordinary number of new models. It shows how dramatically the company's position has changed. Hyundai can now fill gaps in its mainstream range, return to commercial vehicles, develop affordable EVs and hybrids, expand N and continue pushing its core models further upmarket.

But success creates its own challenges. As Hyundai becomes more desirable and technologically ambitious, the boundaries within Hyundai Motor Group become increasingly important — particularly for Genesis.

The opportunity is enormous. Hyundai doesn't need every new model to move upwards, and Genesis doesn't need to produce more expensive versions of cars that already exist elsewhere in the group. Give each brand and each new model a clear purpose, and those 100 launches could make Hyundai's range broader without making it more confusing.

items.title: Stellantis Vans 2030: What Comes Next for Europe's Biggest Van Family?
items.summary: Stellantis has built one of Europe’s biggest commercial vehicle operations, with familiar names from Citroën, Fiat, Peugeot, Opel and Vauxhall covering almost every corner of the van market. But the automotive world is changing faster than the traditionally slow-moving commercial vehicle cycle. Battery technology continues to improve, hybrid powertrains are finding new…
items.content_html:
Stellantis has built one of Europe’s biggest commercial vehicle operations, with familiar names from Citroën, Fiat, Peugeot, Opel and Vauxhall covering almost every corner of the van market. But the automotive world is changing faster than the traditionally slow-moving commercial vehicle cycle. Battery technology continues to improve, hybrid powertrains are finding new applications, connected services are becoming increasingly important, and AI and autonomous driving could eventually transform how goods move altogether.

For Stellantis, the challenge isn't simply replacing today's successful vans. It's deciding what actually needs to change, what is already working, and where entirely new types of commercial vehicle could fit in.

The most intriguing part of Stellantis Pro One’s next chapter may not be a conventional van at all. On 14 September, Stellantis is set to reveal its new autonomous “Box-on-Wheels” concept, giving us a much clearer idea of how the company sees commercial vehicles developing beyond the driver-operated vans we know today.

Its importance could extend far beyond the vehicle itself. Connected fleets, AI-assisted logistics and eventually fully autonomous deliveries could allow Pro One to develop into an entire commercial-vehicle ecosystem, ready to expand as legislation catches up with the technology across Europe and further afield.

The Peugeot Partner, Citroën Berlingo, Vauxhall and Opel Combo and Fiat Doblò already have a winning formula. Stellantis' compact vans are its best-selling van family globally, while in Europe they accounted for an enormous 48.2% of the segment in the first four months of 2026.

After a substantial facelift in 2024, there seems little reason to start again. Stellantis itself is continuing to develop the existing architecture: its new Smart Compact Van retains the same basic platform and dimensions, while a mild-hybrid powertrain is confirmed for 2027. The wider Pro One plan also confirms new LFP and NMC battery technology, aimed at improving both range and affordability.

Our Combo therefore imagines another substantial facelift rather than an all-new van. Lower-cost battery technology, hybrid power and further improvements to an already versatile package could comfortably keep this generation competitive past 2030.

When the current Peugeot Expert and Citroën Dispatch arrived in 2016 alongside the Toyota Proace, the formula was relatively straightforward: a lower, more car-like mid-size van combining useful load space with everyday usability. Since then, that formula has spread much further. The Vauxhall and Opel Vivaro and Fiat Scudo have joined the family, Iveco is now entering the line-up with the eJolly, while Ram is also preparing to bring the architecture to North America. What started as a Peugeot, Citroën and Toyota project has steadily developed into a global mid-size van family sold under an ever-growing collection of badges.

For the next generation, we don't think Stellantis needs to dramatically change what has become a remarkably successful recipe. Today's electric versions already offer competitive range, while remaining relatively affordable compared with many electric van rivals. Stellantis has struck an impressive balance between price, space, versatility and EV capability, wrapped up in a van that feels remarkably car-like on the road.

Diesel isn't disappearing yet, either. Stellantis has only recently introduced a new 2.2-litre diesel across its mid-size van family, producing up to 180hp and 400Nm. While its use in the next generation hasn't been confirmed, such a recent addition makes an evolved version a logical candidate to continue alongside the forthcoming hybrid and electric options.

At the larger end of the range, Stellantis faces an unusual problem: how do you replace a van whose basic design is approaching 20 years old, yet still gets so much right? The Fiat Ducato and its siblings remain hugely competitive, with an exceptionally wide load bay, countless body configurations and a choice of diesel and electric powertrains. Successive updates have added long-range EV options, modern driver assistance and large touchscreens, increasingly disguising the age of the basic architecture.

But starting again completely could create problems of its own. Across Europe, a huge conversion industry has grown around the Ducato family's dimensions and hard points, producing everything from motorhomes and ambulances to minibuses and specialist commercial vehicles. Compatibility has become an advantage in itself, and abandoning it unnecessarily could prove risky.

Stellantis has already confirmed that a new large-van architecture is coming, but our next-generation Ducato deliberately retains the familiar basic body shape and proportions. Underneath is where the bigger changes happen, with a modernised chassis and electrical architecture capable of supporting improved 2.2-litre diesels, hybrid power and the next generation of electric drivetrains.


At the other end of the scale, things are getting just as disruptive. The arrival of the Fiat Tris and products such as the Citroën Ami Cargo show how the traditional van is beginning to shrink. Microcars are a growing part of Europe's urban transport landscape, and their commercial equivalents could make even more sense for short-distance deliveries, maintenance work and businesses that simply don't need a conventional van.

Our Citroën Dyane takes the basic philosophy of the Tris and develops it into a more enclosed, car-like commercial vehicle. The name isn't accidental, either. Dyane and Ami once sat alongside each other in Citroën's range, making Dyane a fitting badge for a practical working relative of today's Ami.

With a small LFP battery, modest performance and around 50–60 miles of real-world-focused urban range, the emphasis isn't on impressive headline figures. It's about keeping purchase price, weight and running costs low, while providing enough payload and weather protection to make it genuinely useful.

Stellantis doesn't need to reinvent the van. In many respects, its greatest advantage is that the foundations are already there: hugely successful compact vans, a mid-size formula that has spread across an ever-growing number of brands, and a large-van family whose dimensions and versatility have become deeply established with operators and conversion specialists across Europe.

The opportunity is in deciding where to evolve and where to disrupt. Hybrid technology can broaden the appeal of existing vans, improving batteries can make EVs more affordable and capable without simply making them heavier, while vehicles such as the Fiat Tris show there is room to think much smaller.

At the other extreme, autonomous technology could eventually change the definition of a commercial vehicle altogether. Stellantis Pro One's future therefore doesn't need one enormous revolution. It needs to protect what already works, improve what can be better, and be ready for the parts of the commercial vehicle world that really are about to change. Image Credit: Stellantis

items.title: Rebuilding Nissan: The Cars That Could Fix Its Confusing European Line-Up
items.summary: Around 20 years ago, Nissan changed the shape of the mainstream car market. The Qashqai replaced the dependable but forgettable Almera and helped turn the crossover into a family-car staple. The Juke followed, proving equally disruptive, while in 2010 the Leaf brought electric motoring to the masses. All three were game-changing cars…
items.content_html:
Around 20 years ago, Nissan changed the shape of the mainstream car market. The Qashqai replaced the dependable but forgettable Almera and helped turn the crossover into a family-car staple. The Juke followed, proving equally disruptive, while in 2010 the Leaf brought electric motoring to the masses.

All three were game-changing cars - and each proved more successful than Nissan initially anticipated. Today, however, the headlines are very different: financial pressure, shrinking model ranges and, most recently, reports of plans for an electric Qashqai being dropped. So, what could turn things around?

At the bottom of Nissan’s new range, the Micra EV is refreshingly easy to understand. Renault has provided strong foundations, but while the closely related Renault 5 majors on retro desirability, the Micra has developed its own USP: value. With the Renault’s £21,495 post-grant price proving difficult to discount, brand-new Micras can already be found for under £19,000, making this a compelling entry point to new-generation EV technology.

It also introduces an oddity in Nissan’s hierarchy. The Micra offers 1,106 litres of luggage capacity with its seats folded, versus 1,052 litres in the considerably larger Leaf. The Leaf remains stylish, exceptionally efficient and technically impressive, but its slippery shape comes at a price. Nissan’s smallest EV unexpectedly highlights why clearer roles further up the range are needed. Photo credit: Nissan

The Micra isn’t the only model raising questions about the Leaf’s place in Nissan’s hierarchy. The forthcoming Juke EV will sit below it on price, wrapping electric technology in a more upright small-SUV body. Nissan hasn’t released final luggage figures, so it’s too early to declare the Juke more practical, but the signs point that way. Today's Juke offers substantially more maximum luggage capacity than the new Leaf, and Nissan says its electric successor will be roomier still.

Alongside the cheaper Micra, it means Nissan could soon have two EVs beneath the £28,849 Leaf offering more conventional shapes and strong everyday usability. That doesn’t make the Leaf a poor proposition. Its USP is increasingly clear: exceptional efficiency, long range and sleek styling. But those qualities come at a price - financially and in outright versatility - making a clearly defined hierarchy increasingly important. Photo credit: Nissan


The Ariya remains an appealing, comfortable and distinctive EV, but as Nissan’s electric flagship it simply doesn’t create enough distance from the cars below it. At 4,595mm long, with a 466-litre boot and 1,350 litres with the seats folded, its practicality is relatively modest. Comparable electric SUVs demonstrate what is possible: the 4,650mm Vauxhall Grandland Electric offers 550 litres, expanding to 1,645 litres, while the MG S6 EV provides a huge 674 litres and 1,910 litres respectively.

None of this makes the Ariya a bad car; it simply feels undersized for the role it has inherited. Our second-generation Ariya moves decisively upwards, creating the space and separation a true Nissan flagship deserves. Image credit: TheNewYardstick Design Studio

Nissan’s current financial pressures mean simply adding another expensive halo EV above the Ariya is unlikely to be the answer. The cancelled electric Qashqai might once have provided the practical family EV to complement the sleeker Leaf, but that now leaves Ariya with a much bigger role to fill. Our solution is to move it upwards. Today’s Ariya is actually smaller than the X-Trail, despite serving as one of Nissan’s most aspirational models in Europe.

The next generation should offer substantially more space, while keeping pricing competitive enough not to abandon existing Ariya buyers. Nissan has already demonstrated the importance of value, cutting Ariya prices substantially in 2025. Our larger Ariya Mk2 builds on that repositioning: more flagship, rather than simply more expensive. Image credit: TheNewYardstick Design Studio


Nissan’s current crossover hierarchy is easy to understand: Juke, Qashqai and X-Trail provide three distinct steps in size and price. But the Juke is now approaching the end of a long life. It remains one of Nissan’s most distinctive designs, yet today’s limited powertrain choice lacks some of the character of earlier generations, when buyers could choose petrol, diesel and even 200hp Nismo derivatives.

With the next-generation Juke moving to electric power, Nissan has an opportunity to rethink what eventually replaces today’s hybrid model. Our solution is Note X: roughly Juke-sized, but more practical, powered by e-POWER technology and priced deliberately below Qashqai. It would preserve an affordable hybrid entry point while allowing the new Juke EV to develop a much clearer identity of its own. Photo credit: Nissan

Our Note X captures some of the thinking behind the original Qashqai and Note: practical, efficient and well-priced family cars that made clever use of relatively compact dimensions. At around Juke size, Note X would prioritise space and usability over style-led packaging, providing an affordable hybrid step beneath Qashqai. Nissan already has suitable technology, with its hybrids producing from around 140hp and Qashqai e-POWER reaching 190hp - comfortably beyond today’s similarly sized Juke.

It wouldn’t need to be revolutionary. Affordable, economical and genuinely practical, Note X could simply give Nissan another easy-to-understand family car, while allowing the new Juke to begin its next chapter as an EV.

Nissan already has plenty of good cars. What its European range increasingly lacks is a completely obvious hierarchy. Our solution adds little complexity: Note X provides the practical hybrid entry point, while a larger Ariya becomes the unmistakable flagship. Between them, Nissan’s existing models are free to play to their individual strengths.

Twenty years after Qashqai changed Nissan’s fortunes, perhaps the answer isn’t another revolution - just making every model’s purpose crystal clear. Image credit: TheNewYardstick Design Studio

items.title: Beat the 76-Plate Hype: 10 Pre-Reg Cars Under £16,000

items.content_html:
With the new 76 registration arriving on 1 September, thousands of buyers will be preparing to collect a brand-new car. But having the latest number plate can come at a considerable cost. Today, the choice of new cars costing less than £16,000 is remarkably limited, with just three models starting below our budget: the Dacia Sandero, Dacia Spring and Leapmotor T03.

Hyundai i20 - Pre-Reg From: £15,990

The Ford Fiesta may have disappeared, but Hyundai still offers a very respectable answer to the traditional small hatchback. The i20 is a proper supermini rather than a city car, with five doors, a generous 352-litre boot and enough rear-seat space to make it a realistic option for a small family.

Its sharp styling has also aged well, giving the i20 considerably more presence than many budget-focused alternatives. Inside, the design is conventional and easy to understand, while Hyundai's five-year, unlimited-mileage warranty provides some additional reassurance for buyers planning to keep their car.

Kia Picanto - Pre-Reg From: £15,025

While it can't handle quite as many duties as its larger i20 cousin, the Picanto still has plenty going for it. Its compact dimensions and low running costs should particularly appeal to younger and urban drivers, while a tight 9.4-metre turning circle makes squeezing into small parking spaces and navigating busy streets considerably easier.

Kia's seven-year, 100,000-mile warranty is another major attraction, providing considerably longer cover than many rivals and making the Picanto an interesting prospect for buyers planning to keep their car.

Fiat 500e - Pre-Reg From: £14,999

Price cuts have already done the 500e a huge favour, while its recent qualification for the full £3,750 Electric Car Grant has made Fiat's once-expensive electric city car considerably easier to recommend. Interior quality is impressive for the money too, giving the 500e a genuinely premium feel that isn't usually associated with this end of the market.

The smaller-battery version offers 115 miles of range, making it best suited to urban use, while the longer-range model can manage up to 199 miles. With 220Nm of instantly available torque and 0-62mph taking just 9.0 seconds, performance is another unexpected advantage at this price.

Renault Clio - Pre-Reg From: £14,985

This is where pre-reg pricing starts to seriously disrupt the usual new-car hierarchy. For essentially the same money as a basic new Dacia Sandero, you can instead have its more upmarket Renault cousin. The Clio shares plenty of Renault Group thinking beneath the surface, but surrounds it with a noticeably more sophisticated package.

Even the affordable Generation trim includes a touchscreen infotainment system, smartphone connectivity and a digital instrument display, while the interior generally looks and feels considerably more expensive than its price suggests. There's useful space for four adults, a generous boot and the refinement expected from a mature supermini.

Dacia Sandero Stepway Extreme - Pre-Reg From: £15,885

Spend another £900, however, and Dacia comes fighting straight back. Rather than the basic Sandero we've used as our new-car benchmark, pre-reg money stretches to the more distinctive Stepway in high-spec Extreme trim, transforming the proposition considerably.

The raised ride height and chunky body cladding give it genuine crossover presence while providing some useful protection from everyday knocks and scrapes. Extreme models add distinctive Copper Brown detailing, black alloy wheels and a surprisingly upmarket-looking interior, while the large 10.1-inch touchscreen makes the smaller display fitted to our bargain Clio suddenly look rather modest.

Citroën C3 - Pre-Reg From: £14,990

Just as the Stepway appears to have reclaimed the value crown, Citroën comes along and steals it again. The reinvented C3 follows a remarkably similar philosophy, combining compact hatchback dimensions with chunky styling, a raised driving position and enough SUV-inspired personality to feel considerably more substantial than its price suggests.

A large 10.25-inch touchscreen brings plenty of technology to the cabin, while Citroën's emphasis on comfort arguably makes an even stronger impression. Soft suspension and supportive seats have helped make the C3 a new benchmark for affordable comfort, while Citroën's We Care programme offers warranty coverage for up to eight years or 100,000 miles.

Toyota Aygo X 1.0 - Pre-Reg From: £15,956

Toyota's smallest car has now gone hybrid, but remaining examples of the outgoing 1.0-litre petrol model shouldn't be overlooked. Its simple three-cylinder engine has developed an excellent reputation for reliability, while impressive real-world fuel economy makes the Aygo X particularly well suited to drivers wanting to keep everyday running costs low.

The boot might be one of the smallest in this company, but the potential warranty certainly isn't. Toyota's Relax programme can provide cover for up to 10 years or 100,000 miles, offering considerable peace of mind for anyone planning to keep their car long term.

Suzuki Swift - Pre-Reg From: £15,990

If you can get past the looks, there's an awful lot to like about the latest Suzuki Swift. Lightweight construction has long been one of its strengths, helping the little Suzuki feel nimble around town while also contributing to impressively low fuel consumption and running costs.

Its mild-hybrid petrol engine adds a little electrical assistance without requiring owners to plug anything in, making the Swift an uncomplicated option for buyers who simply want an economical small car. Suzuki also enjoys a strong reputation for reliability, while the Swift itself has become a household name after decades of providing affordable, lightweight transport.

Vauxhall Corsa - Pre-Reg From: £15,140

One of the biggest names in the supermini class, the Corsa remains a strong all-rounder. Its 100bhp 1.2-litre turbocharged petrol engine provides enough performance to avoid feeling underpowered, while the latest Vizor front end has transformed the design and given Vauxhall's small hatchback considerably more presence. A large touchscreen and familiar, straightforward interior add to its everyday appeal.

But here's where things get interesting. We've found pre-reg Corsa Electrics for just £120 more – roughly the price of two tanks of petrol. For that tiny premium, buyers get 134bhp, instant electric performance and up to 221 miles of range.

MG3 - Pre-Reg From: £13,495

And finally, the biggest bargain of the lot might leave more than £2,500 of our budget untouched. The MG3 is a proper five-door supermini, yet discounted examples can cost less than many considerably smaller city cars.

Its 1.5-litre petrol engine produces 114bhp, giving the MG3 enough performance to comfortably tackle faster roads and longer journeys where some low-powered city cars can begin to feel out of their depth. There's useful passenger and luggage space too, while its larger footprint gives it the road manners expected from a conventional supermini rather than something designed predominantly for urban use.

Fuel economy isn't class-leading and the MG3 isn't the most sophisticated car here, but that's missing the point. For buyers prioritising space, performance and sheer amount of car for their money, £13,495 is exceptionally difficult to argue with.

The New Yardstick Verdict

A new registration plate might look good on the driveway, but these deals demonstrate just how expensive that privilege can be. From established superminis and comfortable family runabouts to surprisingly capable EVs, pre-reg stock completely reshapes what a £16,000 budget can buy. If you're prepared to accept yesterday's registration number, the smart money may be sitting a little further back on the dealer forecourt.
